source.title: Progresses on some open problems related to infinitely many symmetries

accepted.question_text: How can one give concrete physical interpretations for the infinitely many symmetries and conservation laws that arise in integrable systems, beyond the small subset that already have familiar interpretations such as space-time translation invariance, Galilean or Lorentz invariance, scaling invariance, and the conservation of mass, momentum, and energy?

evidence.quote:
Open Problem 1: Physical explanations of infinitely many symmetries and conservation laws
The elucidation of the physical interpretations of the infinitely many symmetries and conservation laws inherent to integrable systems represents a profound and enduring question at the intersection of physics and mathematics. While it is widely acknowledged that integrable systems are characterized by an infinitely many symmetries and conservation laws, only a select few possess explicit, tangible physical interpretations, such as those related to space-time translational invariance, Galilean or Lorentz invariance, scaling invariance, as well as the conservation of mass, momentum, and energy.

accepted.question_text: For integrable nonlinear partial differential equation systems, whose solution spaces have infinitely many degrees of freedom, are the currently known infinitely many symmetries complete, or do additional undiscovered symmetries exist beyond the standard families already generated in the literature?

evidence.quote:
Open Problem 2: Completeness of known infinitely many symmetries
For nonlinear physical systems with finite n freedoms described by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) system, it suffices to identify a finite number of symmetries or conserved quantities, as the general solution of the model possesses a finite number of arbitrary constants. However, for systems with infinitely many freedoms described by partial differential equation (PDE) systems, assessing the completeness of their symmetries is exceedingly challenging.

accepted.question_text: Can generalized symmetries, especially generalized local symmetries rather than only Lie point symmetries or nonlocal symmetry constraints, be used to derive exact multi-wave solutions of integrable partial differential equation systems, in particular multi-soliton solutions and other exact solutions beyond single periodic cnoidal waves, solitary waves, and Painlevé-type solutions?

evidence.quote:
Open Problem 3: Finding multi-wave solutions via generalized symmetries
While symmetries and conservation laws are instrumental in deriving general solutions for integrable ODE systems, the analogous application within the context of integrable PDEs presents a significant challenge. Despite the fact that several Lie point symmetries have been successfully applied to identify single periodic cnoidal wave solutions, including solitary waves, and Painlevé solutions, the utilization of the vast array of general symmetries to find exact solutions in PDE systems is an unresolved issue.

accepted.question_text: Why do some integrable systems appear to be missing generalized symmetries of certain orders, such as the absence of order 6n + 3 symmetries in the Sawada-Kotera and Kaup-Kupershmidt equations, and more generally can even-order or fractional-order generalized symmetries exist for standard integrable equations such as KdV and modified KdV?

evidence.quote:
Open problem 4: Loss of certain orders of generalized symmetries
The existence of an infinitely many symmetries with varying orders in integrable systems is well-documented. However, for certain key integrable systems, specific orders of generalized symmetries appear to be absent. For instance, the Sawada-Kortera (SK) [11] and Kaup-Kupershmidt (KK) [12] equations exhibit generalized symmetries of orders 6n + 1 and 6n + 5 (n = 0, 1, . . . , ∞), yet the 6n + 3 order symmetries are missing. Furthermore, for well-known equations like KdV and MKdV, there are infinitely many generalized symmetries of odd orders. This raises the question of the existence of even order symmetries and, more broadly, the possibility of fractional order symmetries.

accepted.question_text: Given a particular exact solution u0(x, t) of an integrable system, can the action of infinitely many symmetries introduce an infinite sequence of arbitrary constants into that solution, extending the familiar fact that spatial and temporal translation symmetries can introduce finitely many constants such as x0 and t0 into u0(x − x0, t − t0)?

evidence.quote:
Open Problem 5: Arbitrary constants in special solutions via symmetry transformations
It is a well-established principle that for a particular solution of a given system, denoted as u0(x, t), the incorporation of an arbitrary constant is feasible through the application of a symmetry. Specifically, by invoking the invariance under spatial translation in the x-direction and temporal translation in the t-direction, it is possible to seamlessly integrate two arbitrary constants, represented as {x0, t0}. ... The question that arises is whether the leverage of an infinitely many symmetries could permit the introduction of an infinite series of arbitrary constants into a specific solution.
